These can postpone labour for a few days13,14 and the preferred route for starting treatment is subcutane- ous or intravenous infusion.12 Oral or subcutaneous maintenance therapy with beta2 agonists after success- ful treatment of an episode of acute premature labour produces no further benefit15,16 (see also Maintenance Therapy, below). There is little evidence that beta2 ago- nists significantly reduce perinatal mortality rates.17 The patient may experience adverse cardiovascular and met- abolic effects and, in particular, pulmonary oedema has been reported in some women given beta2 agonists in- travenously to suppress labour (see p.1132). It is there- fore essential that the patient’s heart rate and state of hy- dration are carefully monitored throughout infusion. In the event of caesarean section beta blockers may be needed to combat an increased tendency to uterine bleeding. • More recently, calcium-channel blockers have been shown to be effective tocolytics, presumably by their ac- tion on myometrial calcium.12 Most experience con- cerns nifedipine, which has been reported to be at least as effective as, and possibly better than, beta2 agonists or magnesium in delaying labour,18-20 although a systemat- ic review21 considered the quality of many of the studies reporting efficacy to be poor. It has the advantage that it can be given orally,12 and some favour its use as a first- line drug,1,19 although it is not licensed in the UK for this use. Nicardipine has also produced favourable results.22 Others have expressed concern about the safety of calci- um-channel blockers,23 and some suggest that they should be used with caution.2,3 • Atosiban is a peptide analogue of oxytocin with oxyto- cin antagonist properties. A pooled analysis24 of three controlled studies, and a systematic review,25 found atosiban to be as effective as beta agonists in the man- agement of premature labour, with fewer maternal car- diovascular adverse effects. These findings were sup- ported by a large open-label study26 of women treated with atosiban or usual care (usually a beta agonist). Some clinicians favour atosiban as a first-line tocolytic in preference to the traditional drugs.1-3 • In the USA, magnesium sulfate is the most widely used parenteral tocolytic, and is thought to act by calcium antagonism at the neuromuscular junction.12 Although it has been generally considered to be as effective as the beta2 agonists,12 a systematic review27 concluded that it was ineffective at delaying birth or preventing preterm birth, and it has been suggested that tocolytic use of magnesium may be associated with increased paediatric mortality—see p.1681.
